title: Accounting Workflow: How to Build a Better Process for Your Startup
summary: Accounting Workflow: How to Build a Better Process for Your Startup
body_markdown:
As a startup grows, accounting gets more complicated.


A new funding round, changes in payroll, a growing team, new revenue streams, and an expanding R&D program can all add new accounting and tax requirements.


The challenge isn't just getting the books closed each month. It's building an accounting workflow that keeps financial information organized, gives your team visibility into what's happening, and makes tax and financial decisions easier throughout the year.


For a growing startup, that often means combining the right technology, processes, and people. A dedicated CPA team can help make sure those pieces work together as the business changes.


## **What Is an Accounting Workflow?**


An accounting workflow is the process your business uses to collect, review, organize, and report financial information.


A typical workflow may include:


- Recording and categorizing transactions
- Reconciling bank and credit card accounts
- Processing payroll
- Closing the books each month
- Reviewing financial statements
- Preparing for tax filings
- Managing accounts payable and receivable
- Gathering information for tax credits and other tax work


The exact process will vary by company, but the goal is the same: create a repeatable system that keeps your financial information accurate and accessible.


## **What Makes a Good Accounting Workflow?**


A strong accounting workflow isn't just about completing monthly tasks. It's about creating a process that works consistently as your[company grows](https://fondo.com/blog/the-financial-systems-you-need-after-raising-capital) .


Here are six things to consider.


## **1. Give Your Accounting Team the Full Context**


Start by making sure your accounting team understands the information that shapes your financials.


That includes things like:


- Legal entities and ownership structure
- Chart of accounts and accounting policies
- Financing history
- Payroll and employee structure
- Revenue practices
- Major vendors and recurring expenses
- R&D activities


The more context your accounting team has, the less often you'll need to stop what you're doing to explain how the business works.


A good accounting relationship should get more useful over time because the team builds knowledge of your company rather than starting over every month.


## **2. Establish Clear Ownership**


Someone should be accountable for the overall accounting relationship.


For startups, that may include bookkeeping, financial reporting, corporate tax responsibilities, and R&D tax credit work. These areas don't exist in isolation, so it helps when the people responsible for them can work from the same[financial information](https://fondo.com/blog/how-founders-can-extend-runway-before-their-next-raise) and understand how the pieces connect.


This is especially important when you have multiple providers. If your bookkeeper, CPA, and R&D tax credit provider all work independently, someone has to coordinate the handoffs.


Ideally, that person isn't the founder.


## **3. Create a Consistent Monthly Close**


A monthly close shouldn't just be a deadline on the calendar. It should be a repeatable process.


That means reviewing transactions, reconciling accounts, identifying questions, updating the books, and reviewing the resulting financial information on a regular cadence.


A consistent close also makes it easier to catch issues while they're still easy to fix.


Waiting until tax season to figure out why a transaction was categorized a certain way or where a particular expense belongs can turn a small question into a much bigger project.


## **4. Connect Tax Planning to Your Accounting**


[Tax work](https://fondo.com/blog/your-startups-year-end-finance-checklist) is easier when it starts with financial information that's already organized.


Your accounting records can provide important information for corporate tax preparation and, for eligible startups, the R&D tax credit. Payroll, employee information, expenses, and other financial records may all factor into the tax work your company needs to complete.


Keeping these processes connected throughout the year means you aren't trying to reconstruct the company's financial story at tax time.


It also gives your accounting team an opportunity to flag questions earlier, when there's still time to address them.


## **5. Make It Easy to Ask Questions**


Accounting questions don't always show up neatly at month-end.


A founder might need to understand how a new hire affects payroll, how a transaction should be recorded, or what a financing event means for the books.


You should be able to get an answer from someone who already understands the company, rather than submitting a generic support request and explaining the entire situation again.


Direct communication isn't just about getting a faster response. It's about getting an answer that takes the company's history and current circumstances into account.


## **6. Review the Accounting Workflow as Your Business Changes**


Your accounting workflows shouldn't be set in stone.


Certain business events are good opportunities to review whether your current process still works:


- A new fundraising round
- Board or investor reporting
- A major change in headcount
- New revenue or pricing models
- Annual tax filings
- R&D tax credit preparation
- Expansion into a new state or entity


At these points, ask whether your accounting team already has the information it needs or whether you're spending time rebuilding the context yourself.


If you're constantly explaining the same things or manually moving information between systems, it may be time to rethink your process.


## **Where Does Accounting Workflow Automation Fit?**


Accounting workflow automation can take repetitive work off your team's plate.


For example, accounting software can automate or streamline tasks such as transaction categorization, invoice processing, payment reminders, bank feeds, reconciliations, and financial reporting.


But automation isn't a replacement for accounting judgment.


A system can move information from one place to another. It can't always determine whether a transaction was recorded correctly, explain an unusual expense, or understand how a financing event affects your company's financials.


The best approach is usually a combination of automation and human oversight. Automate repetitive tasks where it makes sense, while keeping an experienced accounting team involved in the decisions that require context.


## **What Is Accounting Workflow Management?**


Accounting workflow management is the ongoing process of making sure financial tasks have clear owners, deadlines, review steps, and documentation.


For a growing startup, that can mean establishing a consistent monthly close, determining who reviews financial statements, setting deadlines for tax-related information, and making sure important accounting questions don't get lost between teams.


Good workflow management doesn't have to mean adding more meetings or complicated processes. In many cases, it's simply about making responsibilities clear and creating a process everyone follows consistently.


## **Why Continuity Matters for Startups**


A dedicated accounting team isn't necessarily about having more people involved in your finances. It's about having the right people build knowledge of the business over time.


When the same team handles your account, each monthly close can build on the one before it. Questions can be answered in the context of previous decisions. Tax work can be informed by the financial records maintained throughout the year.


For founders, that can mean fewer handoffs and less time acting as the middleman between different accounting processes.


It also creates a clearer point of accountability. You know who understands the account, who is responsible for the work, and who to go to when something comes up.


## **The Bottom Line**


A better accounting workflow isn't about adding more processes. It's about creating a system that gets easier to manage as your company grows.


Look for an accounting team that understands your business, maintains context from month to month, communicates directly, and can connect your bookkeeping with the tax and financial work that depends on it.


Technology and accounting workflow automation can make repetitive tasks more efficient, but experienced people still play an important role in reviewing the numbers, answering questions, and helping your accounting process adapt as the business changes.
